records.why: The values 500, 1,000 and 1,500 Pa were described as 'measured', but learners cannot measure them with a can and holes; they are calculated as rho x g x h (1,000 x 10 x 0.05 etc., which I recomputed: 500, 1,000, 1,500 Pa). Also, a jet's landing distance is range = 2 x sqrt(depth x height above the landing surface), so it rises with the square root of depth, and if the can stands on the table with the tray beside it the middle jet can land farthest, which would contradict the lesson. Standing the can at the table edge (hole heights nearly equal above the floor) keeps the order 15 cm > 10 cm > 5 cm. Checked by working range = 2*sqrt(h*y) for y = 0.8 m: 0.69 m, 0.57 m, 0.40 m.
records.old: Then introduce the values: "Scientists have measured the pressure: 500 Pa at 5 cm, 1,000 Pa at 10 cm, 1,500 Pa at 15 cm."
records.new: Then introduce the values: "These pressures come from the depth of the water: 500 Pa at 5 cm, 1,000 Pa at 10 cm, 1,500 Pa at 15 cm. In Lesson 6 you will see how to calculate them." Set up so the jets can be compared fairly: stand the can at the table edge and let the jets fall onto the floor or a long tray, so every jet falls from about the same height. Jet distance grows with depth but not in proportion (for depths 5 : 10 : 15 cm expect roughly 1 : 1.4 : 1.7), so do not tell learners that the distances show the pressures; they only show that deeper water pushes harder.
records.reference: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, Chapter 14 Fluid Mechanics (Bernoulli's equation and Torricelli's theorem for efflux speed v = sqrt(2gh))

records.why: Science error: learners were asked to predict and measure which liquid squirts farthest. By Torricelli's law the exit speed v = sqrt(2gh) does not depend on density, so water, salt water and oil at the same depth land at the same distance, and learners would see no difference. The pressure differences are real (rho x g x h = 1,030 x 10 x 0.10 = 1,030 Pa; 1,000 Pa; 920 Pa, recomputed) and a water U-tube would show 1,030/10,000 = 10.3 cm, 10.0 cm and 9.2 cm. The teacher decides whether a funnel, balloon rubber and clear tube are available; if not, present the table and reason from density only.
records.old: Learners observe and measure how far each stream lands on the tray, using a ruler, and record this. They are then given the table of pressures at 10 cm:
records.new: Learners first observe that the three streams land at about the same distance (the speed of a jet depends on depth, not on density), so jets cannot show the effect of density. A simple pressure gauge (a funnel covered with thin balloon rubber, joined by a clear tube to a U-tube of coloured water) is then lowered to 10 cm in each liquid, by the teacher or one group at a time. The water in the U-tube stands highest for salt water (about 10.3 cm), lower for water (10.0 cm) and lowest for oil (9.2 cm); learners measure the differences with a ruler. They are then given the table of pressures at 10 cm:

records.why: Matches the prompt: marks the 300 kPa and 100 kPa as pressure from the water alone and gives the model answer to the new part (d). Also removes a stray closing bracket at the end.
records.value: (a) At the base (pressure from the water alone): P = ρgh = 1,000 x 10 x 30 = 300,000 Pa = 300 kPa. At 10 m: P = 1,000 x 10 x 10 = 100,000 Pa = 100 kPa. Liquid pressure increases with depth because there is more water weight above, so the wall must withstand 300 kPa at the base compared with 100 kPa higher up. That is why it is thicker at the bottom. (b) F = P x A = 101,000 x 0.004 = 404 N upward. This is much larger than the 2.5 N weight of the water, so the cardboard stays in place. Air has weight and so exerts atmospheric pressure on every surface. (c) Small piston area = 5 cm2 = 0.0005 m2, so P = 50 / 0.0005 = 100,000 Pa = 100 kPa. This pressure is transmitted equally through the enclosed fluid (Pascal's principle). Large piston area = 100 cm2 = 0.01 m2, so F = 100,000 x 0.01 = 1,000 N, which is 20 times 50 N. With the knives the force was the same and the area differed, giving different pressures. With the jack the pressure is the same and the area differs, giving different forces. In both cases, area is the key. (d) The pressure is the same in the wide basin and the narrow tube: 1,000 x 10 x 0.10 = 1,000 Pa, because liquid pressure depends on depth and density, not on container shape or amount of liquid. Cooking oil gives 920 x 10 x 0.10 = 920 Pa, less than water, because oil is less dense.

(b) F = P x A = 101,000 x 0.004 = 404 N upward. This is much larger than the 2.5 N weight of the water, so the cardboard stays in place. Air has weight and so exerts atmospheric pressure on every surface. (c) Small piston area = 5 cm2 = 0.0005 m2, so P = 50 / 0.0005 = 100,000 Pa = 100 kPa. This pressure is transmitted equally through the enclosed fluid (Pascal's principle). Large piston area = 100 cm2 = 0.01 m2, so F = 100,000 x 0.01 = 1,000 N, which is 20 times 50 N. With the knives the force was the same and the area differed, giving different pressures. With the jack the pressure is the same and the area differs, giving different forces. In both cases, area is the key.)
records.new: (a) At the base (pressure from the water alone): P = ρgh = 1,000 x 10 x 30 = 300,000 Pa = 300 kPa. At 10 m: P = 1,000 x 10 x 10 = 100,000 Pa = 100 kPa. Liquid pressure increases with depth because there is more water weight above, so the wall must withstand 300 kPa at the base compared with 100 kPa higher up. That is why it is thicker at the bottom. (b) F = P x A = 101,000 x 0.004 = 404 N upward. This is much larger than the 2.5 N weight of the water, so the cardboard stays in place. Air has weight and so exerts atmospheric pressure on every surface. (c) Small piston area = 5 cm2 = 0.0005 m2, so P = 50 / 0.0005 = 100,000 Pa = 100 kPa. This pressure is transmitted equally through the enclosed fluid (Pascal's principle). Large piston area = 100 cm2 = 0.01 m2, so F = 100,000 x 0.01 = 1,000 N, which is 20 times 50 N. With the knives the force was the same and the area differed, giving different pressures. With the jack the pressure is the same and the area differs, giving different forces. In both cases, area is the key. (d) The pressure is the same in the wide basin and the narrow tube: 1,000 x 10 x 0.10 = 1,000 Pa, because liquid pressure depends on depth and density, not on container shape or amount of liquid. Cooking oil gives 920 x 10 x 0.10 = 920 Pa, less than water, because oil is less dense.

records.why: 1,000 N is the weight of about 100 kg, not of a matatu: a 14-seat matatu (Toyota HiAce type) has a gross weight of about 3 tonnes, roughly 25,000 N (checked: 2,500 kg x 10 N/kg). The classroom numbers (50 N, 5 cm2, 100 cm2, 1,000 N) are right for the physics, so they are kept and the load is renamed to something that really weighs 1,000 N (an engine block, about 100 kg). The note says a real garage jack also uses a long handle and a larger piston ratio. Teacher decides: this reframing or rescaling all numbers (for example 5 cm2 : 500 cm2 for 10,000 N).
records.old: lifts a heavy matatu with a hydraulic jack using only a 50 N push, yet the matatu needs about 1,000 N to be lifted.
records.new: lifts a heavy engine block with a small workshop hydraulic jack using only a 50 N push, yet the engine block needs 1,000 N (about 100 kg) to be lifted. A whole matatu weighs about 25,000 N, so a real garage jack also uses a long handle and a larger piston ratio; the classroom numbers are a simplified model of the same idea.

records.why: The sequence had no language support for English learners and no Kiswahili terms (guideline 12). Teachers must check the Kiswahili terms with local usage before they go on the wall; I could not verify them against a Kiswahili physics glossary.
records.old: Use the name 'pressure' and no other term.
records.new: Use the name 'pressure' and no other term. Build a word wall with Kiswahili support for English learners: pressure (shinikizo), force (nguvu), area (eneo), weight (uzito); add density (msongamano), depth (kina) and atmospheric pressure (shinikizo la angahewa) when they arise. Let learners explain first in Kiswahili or their home language, then in English, with the frame 'The ___ face has a smaller area, so the pressure is ___.'
records.group_headline: No supports for English learners or learners with special needs; added a Kiswahili word wall and sentence frame, more than one way to show the model, and a number support for the calculation lesson

records.why: Guideline 12 asks for accommodations for learners with special needs and more than one way to show understanding; there were none.
records.old: Do not give formulas or numerical calculations.
records.new: Do not give formulas or numerical calculations. Offer more than one way to show the model: learners may talk it through, build it with objects, or label a teacher-drawn outline instead of drawing freehand; give sentence starters ('My idea is that ...') and seat learners with low vision or hearing difficulty close to the demonstration.

records.why: Lesson 3 is the heaviest calculation lesson and offered no support for learners who struggle with unit conversion (guideline 12).
records.old: and to always write units.
records.new: and to always write units. For learners who find powers of ten hard, allow a calculator and a pinned conversion strip (mm to m, cm2 to m2), or pair them with a stronger partner; accept answers given aloud or on a number line.

records.why: Guideline 6 asks that each model's limits are stated. The 2 MPa 'gives way' value is an assumed teaching value and the knife-edge area is simplified; saying so keeps the numbers honest without changing any calculation.
records.old: Correct the language: use 'pressure', not 'stress' or 'strength'.
records.new: Correct the language: use 'pressure', not 'stress' or 'strength'. State the limits of the model: 2 MPa is a round classroom value chosen for teaching (real tomato skin and meat vary), the edge area = length x thickness is a simplification of a curved edge, and cooks also slice with a sliding motion, which helps cutting.

records.why: The CBE rubric levels are Exceeds, Meets, Approaches and Below Expectations. The contract allows only three level fields, so the level names Exceeds, Meets and Approaches Expectations now start the three descriptors; the wording of each descriptor is unchanged.

value.criterion: Claim and use of the key idea (same force, different area)
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: States a clear claim that the difference is the area, not the force, uses the words 'same force, different area', and links pressure to force and area correctly.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: States that area is different and pressure is greater for the sharp knife, but the idea that force is the same is missing or unclear.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Claim is missing, or says the sharp knife uses more force, or gives no link to pressure.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: All areas and pressures are correct (5 x 10^-6 m2, 5 x 10^-5 m2, 8 MPa, 0.8 MPa) with correct unit conversions and units throughout the other calculations.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Method is correct but there is one small error in conversion or units.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Several errors or missing units, or P = F/A is not used correctly.

value.criterion: Use of evidence and threshold reasoning
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Compares 8 MPa and 0.8 MPa with the 2 MPa value to explain cutting versus squashing, and supports the idea with evidence from the brick, camel and other lessons.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses the knife numbers but uses the 2 MPa value or other lessons' evidence only partly.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives little or no evidence, or does not use the 2 MPa value.

value.criterion: Extension to liquids, air and hydraulics
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Correctly calculates and explains dam pressure, the air force on the glass and the jack, and clearly contrasts the jack (same pressure, different area) with the knives.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Calculates most of these correctly but explanations are brief or the contrast with the knives is weak.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Calculations or explanations are mostly missing or incorrect.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Compares the Lesson 1 model with the final model, naming what stayed, what changed and which lessons caused it, in clear organised sentences.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Describes some changes to the model but with few links to lessons.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Does not compare the models or the writing is unclear.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations) but the partner contract has only three level fields (excellent, proficient, developing), so Below Expectations cannot be written into the data. Suggest the partner template adds a fourth field, or teachers add the level by hand when printing.

Sub-strand number mismatch: this sequence is labelled Sub-Strand 1.1 Pressure throughout, but in the KICD Grade 10 Physics design 'Pressure' is sub-strand 1.2 (1.1 is Introduction to Physics). Not renamed, as instructed; the number should be confirmed with the teachers and the partner.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Physics, Strand 1.0 Mechanics and Thermal Physics, sub-strand 'Pressure' (numbered 1.2 in KICD)

records.why: KICD content and outcomes not taught or not yet tied to an activity: bicycle pump and mechanisms of water pumping (only the optional Lesson 9 homework search); the garage visit to see a braking system and the discussion of car-tyre pressure against vehicle loading; the PCIs climate change and General History of Africa (wind patterns and Indian Ocean trade). KICD suggests 19 lessons for this sub-strand and the sequence has 9, so a short extra lesson or a field/project task could cover them. Suggested placement if a teacher wants it in the existing lessons: tyre pressure and loading as a short discussion in Lesson 8; air pressure and weather (climate change) in Lesson 7's Driving Question Board step. Also KICD does not list pressure in solids; Lessons 1-3 are the teachers' anchor and are kept.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Physics, Strand 1.0 Mechanics and Thermal Physics, sub-strand 'Pressure' (numbered 1.2 in KICD)
